candidates.quote: It is justice, not charity, that is wanting in the world!
candidates.author: Mary Wollstonecraft
candidates.work: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
candidates.locator: Chapter 4 (Observations on the State of Degradation to Which Woman Is Reduced by Various Causes)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A morning corrective for the month: kindness that stops at almsgiving has not yet widened the circle, and what the world wants first is fairness.

candidates.quote: The good we secure for ourselves is precarious and uncertain, is floating in mid-air, until it is secured for all of us and incorporated into our common life.
candidates.author: Jane Addams
candidates.locator: Chapter VI, The Subjective Necessity for Social Settlements (her 1892 essay, reprinted); Macmillan, 1910
candidates.whyThisMonth: The widest possible circle stated as plain fact: my good is not safe until it is everyone’s, which is the working definition of compassion for a whole day.

candidates.quote: The greatest benefit we owe to the artist, whether painter, poet, or novelist, is the extension of our sympathies.
candidates.author: George Eliot
candidates.work: The Natural History of German Life
candidates.locator: Westminster Review, July 1856; in The Essays of George Eliot, ed. Nathan Sheppard (Funk and Wagnalls, 1883), essay V, p. 141 ff.
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month’s blurb in one sentence from the novelist herself: art exists to stretch our sympathy toward people unlike us.

candidates.quote: To will oneself free is also to will others free.
candidates.author: Simone de Beauvoir
candidates.locator: Part II, Personal Freedom and Others (Philosophical Library, 1948)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Nine words that turn a private wish into a public one: whatever I want for my own morning I owe to the next person.

candidates.quote: Forgiving, in other words, is the only reaction which does not merely re-act but acts anew and unexpectedly, unconditioned by the act which provoked it and therefore freeing from its consequences both the one who forgives and the one who is forgiven.
candidates.author: Hannah Arendt
candidates.locator: Chapter V, section 33, Irreversibility and the Power to Forgive (University of Chicago Press, 1958), p. 241
candidates.whyThisMonth: Forgiveness reframed as the one free act in the day: it releases the forgiver as much as the forgiven, which is compassion with a mechanism.

candidates.quote: Ultimately, we have just one moral duty: to reclaim large areas of peace in ourselves, more and more peace, and to reflect it towards others.
candidates.author: Etty Hillesum
candidates.work: An Interrupted Life: The Diaries of Etty Hillesum 1941–1943
candidates.locator: Diary entry of 29 September 1942 (Pantheon paperback, 1984, p. 185)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Kindness begins as housekeeping inside oneself before six, and the diary says the peace made there is meant to be passed on.

candidates.quote: I feel at home in the entire world wherever there are clouds and birds and human tears.
candidates.author: Rosa Luxemburg
candidates.locator: Written from Wronke prison; The Letters of Rosa Luxemburg, ed. Georg Adler, Peter Hudis and Annelies Laschitza (Verso, 2011), p. 376
candidates.whyThisMonth: Fellow-feeling with no border on it: a letter from a cell that refuses to sort suffering by nation, which is the circle at its widest.

candidates.quote: The love of our neighbor in all its fullness simply means being able to say to him: ‘What are you going through?’
candidates.author: Simone Weil
candidates.locator: Reflections on the Right Use of School Studies with a View to the Love of God (1942), in Waiting for God (Putnam, 1951)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Compassion reduced to one question you can actually ask someone today; a backup for the Weil carry-in should its page citation fail, since one Weil line is the month’s limit.

candidates.quote: How selfish soever man may be supposed, there are evidently some principles in his nature, which interest him in the fortune of others, and render their happiness necessary to him, though he derives nothing from it except the pleasure of seeing it.
candidates.author: Adam Smith
candidates.locator: Part I, Section I, Chapter I, Of Sympathy: the opening sentence of the book
candidates.whyThisMonth: The famous economist opens his first book by saying we are built to care about other people’s happiness for no return at all: a good thing to believe before breakfast.

candidates.quote: Yet minds are not conquered by force, but by love and high-mindedness.
candidates.author: Baruch Spinoza
candidates.whyThisMonth: For the day that will contain an argument: the only thing that ever changes another mind is generosity, and the geometer says so.

candidates.author: Martin Buber
candidates.locator: Part One (T. and T. Clark, 1937), p. 11
candidates.whyThisMonth: Five words that make every encounter of the coming day the point of the day rather than an interruption of it.

candidates.quote: Boundless compassion for all living beings is the surest and most certain guarantee of pure moral conduct, and needs no casuistry.
candidates.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
candidates.locator: Part III, Chapter VIII, The Proof Now Given Confirmed by Experience, section (4); section 19 in the German
candidates.whyThisMonth: The pessimist’s one warm doctrine, and the month’s thesis: compassion is not an ornament on ethics but the whole of it, and it needs no rulebook.

candidates.quote: No man is devoid of a heart sensitive to the suffering of others.
candidates.author: Mencius
candidates.locator: Book II, Part A, 6 (2A6), the opening sentence, before the child at the well
candidates.whyThisMonth: The oldest argument that compassion is standard equipment, not a rare virtue: a reader wakes already possessing what the month asks for.

candidates.quote: All the joy the world contains / Has come through wishing happiness for others. / All the misery the world contains / Has come through wanting pleasure for oneself.
candidates.author: Shantideva
candidates.whyThisMonth: Four lines that reverse the usual morning arithmetic: the day goes better for wanting someone else’s to; a treatise by a named author, not scripture.

candidates.quote: The good life is one inspired by love and guided by knowledge.
candidates.author: Bertrand Russell
candidates.locator: Chapter II, The Good Life (E. P. Dutton, 1925), pp. 19 to 20; set in italics as his creed
candidates.whyThisMonth: A whole ethics in eleven words, with love placed first and knowledge second; the logician’s own order of priority for a day.

candidates.quote: The best way to begin a day well is to think, on awakening, whether we cannot give pleasure during the day to at least one person.
candidates.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
candidates.locator: Volume I, section 589, The Day’s First Thought (T. N. Foulis, 1909)
candidates.whyThisMonth: Literally a six-in-the-morning instruction: decide on waking whom you will be kind to today, from the last author anyone expects it of.
